notes.note: تَعْبَان (taʿbān) is the colloquial word for 'tired'; MSA uses مُتْعَب (which day 46 then teaches) or تَعِب. Not wrong in a polite everyday dialogue, but the two days now teach two different words for the same idea.
'salāmtik to a woman' is the colloquial pronunciation; the MSA form the course teaches on day 43 is سَلَامَتُكِ (salāmatuki). Consider aligning the two culture notes.

رَكِبَ عَلَى الْحِمَار is attested in classical and modern Arabic (رَكِبَ عَلَى الدَّابَّة); رَكِبَ الْحِمَار is more common, but calling the عَلَى version a mistake is too strong. Perhaps present it as 'the usual way' rather than wrong.

The wrong (ثَلَاثَة مَرَّات) and right (ثَلَاثَ مَرَّات) forms both transliterate as 'Thalātha marrāt' because ة in pause is -a. The learner sees two identical ⟶ lines under two different Arabic strings; a transliteration 'thalāthat' or an explicit note would make the difference audible.

لَازِم أَنْ is a colloquial-flavoured construction; in careful MSA one says يَجِبُ أَنْ or مِنَ اللَّازِمِ أَنْ. The intro flags يَجِبُ as 'more formal', which covers it, but 'In standard Arabic lāzim needs an' presents لَازِم itself as standard.
The English adds 'all day' ('I'll be busy all day on Saturday'); the Arabic says only سَأَكُونُ مَشْغُولًا يَوْمَ السَّبْت.
The English ends 'See you on Sunday!' while the Arabic is إِلَى اللِّقَاء ('see you'); harmless but not literal.
The tap gloss يَد=hand ('hand luggage') carries an odd parenthetical from another lesson; 'hand' alone would be clearer here.
سَامِي يَسْبَحُ فِي النَّادِي is tagged 'nominal-sentence'; it is a subject + verbal predicate. Only affects the grammar link, not the Arabic.

summary: Checked every Arabic string in days 41-50 (titles, intros, sentences with their mistakes, dialogues, readings, quizzes, culture notes) for harakat, case endings, jussive after لَمْ, subjunctive after أَنْ, imperatives and negative imperatives, dual forms, feminine body parts, faʿlān/faʿlā adjectives, numbers 3-10 and 20-99, plus every seg and tap gloss, every ⟶ transliteration and every answer key. The core Arabic of the lessons is sound: no misspelt word, wrong verb form or wrong answer key was found, and the grammar rules taught (لَمْ + jussive, verb before plural subject stays singular, أَنْ + -a, ʿaṭshān → ʿaṭshā, 3-10 opposite gender) are correct. All 13 findings are in the tap-gloss dictionary and the transliteration engine rather than in the lessons themselves: 4 major gloss errors where a tapped word shows the wrong sense or wrong gender/tense (سَلَامَتُكِ labelled 'to a man', تَفْتَحُ glossed as passive, مَا glossed 'what' in a negation lesson, يَحْضُرُ glossed as past), 9 minor items (ة rendered 'A / at', 'Wasāmī'-style capitalisation of names after wa-/li-, 'Shāī' for shāy, garbled imperative glosses, glosses copied from another lesson's sense, and an imperative rule in the day 44 intro that omits the helping alif). The pattern is that the one-word tap dictionary reuses a single gloss across all senses and tenses of a word, so each new grammar point (negation مَا, jussive vs indicative, imperative vs statement) inherits glosses from the lesson where the word first appeared. Notes cover register (تَعْبَان, salāmtik, لَازِم), one over-strict 'mistake' (رَكِبَ عَلَى), and small English additions.
